1116: Part B – A colleague is in distress. The aim is not to find the perfect words, but to create a safe context where the other person can talk, if they wish.
1122: How to start, how to be and how to respect their pace
1123: Approaching a colleague in distress does not require a complex intervention, but a clear, respectful approach that fits the moment.
1129: Be direct, simple and respectful. Mention what you have observed and leave room for a reply.
1130: “I noticed you don’t seem as well and I wanted to know how you are.”
1131: “I’ve noticed you seem more overwhelmed. Would you like to talk for a bit?”
1133: Use a less direct approach if you are not that close.
1134: “I just wanted to see how you are – is everything OK?”
1135: “If you need to talk, I’m around.”
1137: Keep a calm tone, without rushing or dramatising. Give the person time to reply.
1138: “We can talk calmly, there’s no hurry.”
1139: “I’m here to listen, with no pressure.”
1141: Show presence through how you are (not only through what you say).
1144: Keep your attention on the other person
1146: Respect it if the person does not want to talk at that moment.
1147: “That’s fine if you don’t want to talk now.”
1148: “If another time suits you better, we can talk later.”
1151: “If you change your mind, I’m available.”
1152: “You don’t have to explain more than you want to.”
1156: The conversation is the central moment of the intervention. It is not about solving the situation, but about creating a safe space where the person can express themselves. These dimensions are not rigid stages, but guidelines that complement one another throughout the interaction.
1157: Dimensions of support during the conversation
1162: Listening is more than hearing words. It means genuine attention to what the person says, to what they do not say and to how they express themselves.
1163: The aim is not to respond quickly, but to understand.
1164: Effective listening conveys an implicit message: “what you are going through matters and deserves attention”.
1165: When listening, it is important to
1166: Give the person time to speak, without interrupting
1167: Avoid anticipating or finishing their sentences
1168: Focus on what the person considers relevant
1169: Accept moments of silence, without rushing to fill them
1172: “You can speak at your own pace.”
1173: “Would you like to tell me what has been hardest?”
1175: Validating means recognising the person’s emotional experience as legitimate, without judging, correcting or relativising it. It does not mean agreeing with everything, but showing understanding.
1176: Validation is particularly important because it reduces the feeling of isolation and helps the person feel understood.
1177: When validating, it is important to
1178: Name or reflect emotions when appropriate
1181: “It makes sense that you feel this way.”
1183: “I understand that this has affected you.”
1184: “It’s understandable that you feel this way in this situation.”
1185: Supporting means helping the person deal with the present moment, without taking control of the situation. The focus is on facilitating, not solving.
1187: Practical: small, concrete actions (e.g. helping to make a call, finding a quiet space)
1188: Looking to the near future: helping to think about the “next step”, without pressing
1189: When supporting, it is important to
1190: Ask what the person needs, instead of assuming
1191: Offer concrete help, but do not impose it
1192: Respect the person’s pace and decisions
1193: “How can I support you right now?”
1194: “Is there anything that would help you now?”
1195: “Would you like us to stay here for a bit?”
1198: Not everyone will want to talk a lot. Some people may need time to organise what they are feeling.
1200: 1Silence should not be seen as a failure
1201: 2Presence is still a form of support
1202: 3Short phrases of continuity can help
1204: “You don’t have to say anything, I can just stay here with you.”
1205: “We can stay in silence, if you prefer.”
1206: “You don’t have to explain more than you want to.”
1207: “If you want to talk later, I’m available.”
